U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert is flatly denying claims made in an ethics complaint filed by a persistent political critic alleging the Windsor Republican had affairs with multiple members of her congressional staff in violation of House rules and arranged for a $200,000 payment to keep a former staff member quiet. A complaint filed late last week with the House Committee on Ethics by David Wheeler, who runs North Carolina-based American Muckrakers PAC, called for an investigation into what he alleged were lengthy relationships between Boebert and three staff members, including her former district director, a former chief of staff and her current chief of staff. A House rule adopted in 2018 forbids lawmakers from engaging in sexual relationships with supervised employees. Boebert, 39, was first elected to represent Colorado's Western Slope-based 3rd Congressional District in 2020. She moved to the more reliably Republican 4th Congressional District, which covers the Eastern Plains, ahead of the 2024 election and is seeking a fourth term. "I reject these baseless allegations as utterly false and there is no truth to them whatsoever," Boebert said in a written statement. "I have never had a sexual relationship or an inappropriate romantic relationship with any member of my staff — past or present. This is nothing more than a politically motivated stunt designed to manipulate the ethics process, create headlines, smear me, and generate clickbait." "This was a political smear packaged as an ethics filing and published before anyone checked whether it even qualifies under the committee's rules," Boebert said. Calling Wheeler's allegations "ridiculous, reckless and politically motivated," Boebert insisted the complaint failed to satisfy the ethics panel's rules, which she said require a House member to cosign complaints submitted by nonmembers. U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert, a Windsor Republican, calls out the media for reporting on an ethics complaint filed against her in a video posted online on Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026. (via X) In a video posted online Sunday afternoon, Boebert went further, calling Wheeler's complaint a "scam" and accusing media outlets that ran with the story over the weekend of crossing a line by reporting on the staff members implicated in the filing. Claiming that his sources possess text messages, recorded conversations and bank records to back up the allegations, Wheeler also said that one of the former congressional employees, former state Sen. Clarice Navarro, who served as Boebert's district director from 2021 until early 2025, received a $200,000 payment to "secure her silence" after she threatened to expose the relationship. Navarro denied the allegations, calling Wheeler's claims "entirely false and defamatory" in a statement to the Colorado Times-Recorder. Boebert's former chief of staff, Jeff Small, who ran her congressional office from early 2021 until 2025, called the allegations "categorically false and defamatory" in a cease-and-desist email obtained by Colorado Politics that was sent to Wheeler on Saturday by a Colorado law firm. Wheeler doubled down on the allegations contained in the complaint late Tuesday in written statements to Colorado Politics and a formal cease-and-desist letter sent to Boebert and her current staff. The letter demands they issue corrections and retract statements accusing Wheeler of committing perjury by knowingly filing false statements in his complaint. Citing North Carolina law surrounding defamation lawsuits, Wheeler told Boebert and her staff to preserve all documents related to the ethics complaint. "If the requested corrections are not made, I will consider pursuing the legal remedies available to me," Wheeler added. In an email to Colorado Politics, Wheeler said the letter puts Boebert and her staff on notice that he's considering legal action related to their forceful denials of his accusations. A spokesman for Boebert didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from Colorado Politics regarding Wheeler's latest communication. Wheeler also disputed Boebert's contention that the ethics committee was unable to consider his allegations in an email to Colorado Politics, saying that the panel can decide to look into complaints brought to its attention by any source. He added that he is "in discussions" with at least five House members who are interested in signing on to the complaint but acknowledged that their campaigns are "causing the holdup." "This delay does not in any way interfere with our complaint," Wheeler added. "It is before the Committee as a citizen-submitted complaint."
